$$\\[1cm]$$
**Research question:**
- Do wars make ordinary people more aggressive toward nationals of the enemy country online?

<blockquote>Or, is war "just politics"?</blockquote>


- An RCT to answer this research question is unfeasible.
- Data from individuals' interactions, while their countries are at war against each other? Anectodal evidence from sports.

--
- Online platforms?

--
- [chess.com](https://chess.com) operates 24/7! (the biggest online chess platform)
  - ~30,000 games happen each hour worldwide
  
---

# Conflicts

Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) Dyadic Dataset version 23.1

- Two "countries"
- "Substantial" military involvement (>1,000 number of soldiers actively engaged)
    - Excluding (for now) small "border clashes", e.g., between India and Pakistan, China...
- Since 2010 (that's when chess.com's data becomes available)

---

# Summary
- We web-scraped games played by Armenian, Azerbaijani, Ukrainian, Russian, Israeli, and Palestinian players before and after the start of conflict

  - Arm-Az: ~131,000 games with 20,000 during conflict
  - Ukr-Ru: ~1,142,000 games with 520,000 during conflict
  - Isr-Pal: ~52,000 games with 22,000 during conflict

- Outcomes we look at
  - Do hostile players play more aggressively? Performance?
  - Mechanisms? Does the impact depend on who initiated the war, army size, public support?
  - Behavioral angle: Loss aversion, ie, prospect theory.
  
- Results
  - Hostile pairings are more likely to be "fighting" games, but not necessarily more aggressive. Less resignations, more checkmates.
  - Consistent with loss aversion: players value "not losing" $>$ wining.
  - Effects are strongest for the Ukraine-Russia pairings.
  - Lasts for <4 months

---

# Relevant Literature

- Conflicts alter perception and foster identity: Akerlof and Kranton (2000, QJE), Caceres-Delpiano et. al. (2021, JPubE), Gehring (2022, EJ), among others.
  - Dawson and Dabson (2010, JEconPsych): Referee bias by nationality
  - Depetris-Chauvin et. al. (2020, AER): Africa Cup of Nations & civil conflict

- Emotional responses to "news": 
  - Sharkey and Shen (2021, PNAS): Mass shootings in the U.S.
  - Guo and An (2022, JDevE): Terrorist attacks in Africa

- Performance under "stress": Cahlíková et. al. (2020, MS) etc.

# A simple model

$$U_{y, i, j}  = \alpha_y+\beta_{y, j} \quad y\in\{win, draw, loss\}$$

where $U_{y, i, j}$ is the utility player $i$ obtains from outcome $y$ against opponent $j$. Assume 

$$\begin{align}\label{eq:2}
    y =\begin{cases}
     win & \text{with probability } p(a) \\
     loss & \text{with probability } q(a) \\
     draw & \text{with probability } 1-p(a)-q(a)
    \end{cases}
\end{align}$$

$$\small\begin{align}\label{eq:5}
    &\max_{a} \mathbb{E}[U_{y, i, j}] \\
    &\max_{a} p(a)\big(\alpha_{win}+\beta_{win, j}\big) +\big(1-p(a)-q(a)\big)\big(\alpha_{draw}+\beta_{draw, j}\big)+q(a)\big(\alpha_{loss}+\beta_{loss, j}\big)  \nonumber
\end{align}$$

$\Rightarrow$ Aggression: More pleasure from beating a hostile opponent raises aggression, but an isolated increase in disutility from losing against a hostile opponent lowers aggression. (ambiguous net effect)

$\Rightarrow$ Performance: Improves with effort, but declines with mental pressure/stress with playing against an opponent from hostile nation. (ambiguous net effect)

Gandhi et al (2024, NBER): Beliefs that entertain (LA, spite, suspense/surprise)

# Chess data: Aggression
- Aggressiveness/"risk level" of a chess game? 
  - Gerdes and Gransmark (2010, Labour Econ); Dreber et. al. (2013, JEBO): opening strategy. Deviation from usual opening score: $I_{i} = -\log\left(\frac{n_{ie}}{N_{i}}\right)$
  - Certain aggressive moves, eg, number of checks (attacking the King) or Queen captures
  - Decisiveness of games

- <b>Empirical Strategy:</b> Differences in Differences
  - Each row is from the pov of a hostile player, ie Ukrainian, Russian..
  - Hostile: eg, Ukrainian vs. Russian pairing
  - Control: their games against neutral countries
  - pre/post conflict start
- No variation in treatment timing: post same for everyone.
- How do users get matched? Random. BUT, can someone "refuse" to play? Yes. (biases results towards zero) BUT we do not see evidence of refusals.

# Chess data: Diff in Diff

$Y_{ijg} = \gamma (H_{ij} \times \text{Post}_g) + \delta H_{ij} + \lambda \text{Post}_g + \pmb{X_{ijg}}'\pmb{\beta} + \alpha_i + u_{ijg}$

where $H_{ij}$ equals 1 if players $i$ and $j$ are from "hostile" country pairs; $\text{Post}_g$ equals 1 if game $g$ occurred after the conflict start date; $H_{ij} \times \text{Post}_g$ is the DiD interaction term with $\gamma$ the coefficient 
of interest. $\alpha_i$ is player FEs; $u_{ijg}$ is the idiosyncratic shock.

$Y_{ijg}$ includes performance e.g., mistakes, blunders; game outcomes e.g., decisive games vs. draws; and other aggressive moves.

- Mechanisms: "How the game ended": e.g., "agree" to a draw, "stalling" a game; game length (measured by total number of moves).

# Discussion and Conclusion

- We study how wars affect behavior between civilians from opposing sides using >40 million moves made on the biggest chess platform: chess.com

  - Hostile pairings play more *combative* games after conflict: longer, more checks, more queen captures, more checkmates, fewer resignations
  - Players deviate more from their usual opening repertoire to minimize ambiguity
  - Performance mildy *better*: controlled aggression, no reckless play
  - Most players accept a game against a randomly matched hostile opponent, but a number of them who accept resign after, ie abandon on a roughly even position
  - Effects strongest for Ukraine-Russia: largest scale and most devastating conflict
  - Smaller country players (Armenia, Ukraine, Palestine) show stronger fighting response
  - Effects are consistent across skill levels and time controls

- One application: Real-time measurement of public response to war.
